fix.shows: A research intern with Jean Dreze reports from the hearings at the Ranchi collectorate on 2 September, from two booth level officers, one at a booth in urban Ranchi and one at a rural booth in Bagodar, and from the published lists of unmapped electors for two booths in Hatia. He reports that people who came with only a voter ID card and Aadhaar were asked for a caste or residence certificate, and that stalls outside drew up affidavits for Rs 300 to Rs 500 each, though as far as he could tell most were not needed. He puts the minimum wage for unskilled work in Jharkhand's larger cities at about Rs 520 a day, so that an affidavit can cost most of a day's pay. He reports that about two in five of the 172 unmapped electors on the two Hatia lists are women recorded only through a husband's name, and that over half of them are 41 or older. The booth level officers name migrant workers, women who cannot produce a parent's entry and tenants in urban areas as the electors most easily lost, and he reports that many elderly electors who received notices cannot keep travelling to the office. One of the officers describes an Election Commission portal whose server often goes down. He cites the Chief Electoral Officer's office for 63,24,116 electors on the draft roll to be served notices, and for Hatia as the constituency with the most notices, 1,52,362. He says the account rests on two booths, two booth level officers and one visit, and makes no claim beyond them.
